title: Thorn's Brave Song
markdown:
The sun was a warm blanket over the Endless Plains, stretching further than a hawk could ever fly. A very blue sky stretched wide above. Here, nestled amongst a whispering sea of green and gold grass, lived Thorn the thrush. Thorn had a song. It was bright and cheerful, like a fresh buttercup. His song could even make a grumpy badger smile. But Thorn held a little secret. He felt shy whenever he looked down from too high up. The ground looked so very, very far away, and his tummy did a little flutter.

His very good friend, Pecan the prairie dog, was quite the opposite. Pecan was full of energy and always sure of himself, a whirlwind of activity. His little paws were a blur as he dug new tunnels, kept his burrow very tidy, and carefully sorted his pantry, making sure it was always stocked with the best seeds. Pecan was sensible through and through. If a sunflower seed was not perfectly arranged, Pecan arranged it again.

One hazy afternoon, as the sky took on orange and rose, a rustle high above announced Elder Hoot. This was no ordinary owl. His feathers were the deep silent black of a moonless night. He landed with surprising grace on the tip of a tall grass stalk, amber eyes gleaming. “A warning,” he boomed, a rumble through the roots. “A great herd of buffalo, hooves like a thousand drums, is thundering this way. They move faster than anyone can imagine.”

Elder Hoot held out one claw. On it sat a tiny gleaming whistle: the legendary Whistle of Whispers, which could carry a sound far and wide, even against a strong breeze. “Thorn. You must take this to the prairie dog town. Warn them before the earth itself begins to tremble.”

Thorn’s small heart flip-flopped. “Me?” His bright voice went thin. “The grass is so tall. It sways. And the wind pushes and pulls.”

“You are swift,” Elder Hoot said, gentle and firm. “And your heart is true. That is what matters most.” He placed the whistle in Thorn’s beak. Cool. Smooth.

Thorn knew, deep down, that he had to do this. He looked out at the endless rolling green sea. The prairie dog town, he knew, was just beyond the tallest grass. That place always made his tummy do a little somersault. He took a deep breath, a really deep breath for such a tiny creature, filling his little lungs with the fresh prairie air.

He launched himself into the sky. For the first few moments it felt just fine. He flapped his wings with a familiar comforting rhythm, rising steadily. Then a gust of wind, playful and strong, swooped in. It nudged him sideways, first gently, then not so gently. The grass below, which had been swaying gently, now looked like a wild green sea tossing in a storm. Thorn felt himself pushed this way and that. His wings flapped harder, trying to find their rhythm again. He felt a dizzying wobble. His tummy did another, bigger flip. For just a fleeting second he squeezed his eyes shut tight. Pecan and all his friends were counting on him.

He remembered Elder Hoot’s words. He opened his eyes, gaze sharp and focused, and fixed them on the distant horizon. He could just make out Pecan’s familiar burrow entrance now, a tiny dark speck against the vibrant green. He flew with all his might, his wings beating a determined powerful rhythm against the insistent push of the wind.

A new sound ripped through the air. A low continuous rumble that sent shivers down his tiny spine: the distant thunder of hooves. The buffalo were much closer than he had thought. He had to be faster.

Thorn dived. He swooped, a streak of brown against the green, flying remarkably low, just above the tallest waving stalks of grass. His heart pounded a frantic rhythm against his ribs. The height was still there. He kept the whistle and the speck and did not look at the drop. He reached Pecan’s burrow, landing with a final breathless flutter.

Pecan had been arranging a particularly large and perfect sunflower seed. He looked up, startled.

“Pecan. Warning,” Thorn gasped, dropping the whistle at Pecan’s paws. “Buffalo. A stampede.”

Pecan’s eyes widened for a split second. He did not panic. He nudged the whistle with his nose. A sharp clear blast sliced the air and echoed across the plains. He added his own urgent squeak. A flurry of squeaks answered from every direction. In moments every prairie dog, from the littlest pup to the oldest elder, had scurried deep into well-built burrows.

Just as the last prairie dog vanished underground, the ground began to shake, not just a little tremor, but a deep powerful vibration. A magnificent wave of brown shaggy shapes thundered past, their breath a mighty gale, their hooves shaking the very earth as if it were a flimsy drum. The prairie dog town, thanks to Thorn, remained silent and perfectly secure beneath the chaos.

When the last fading hoofbeat had finally disappeared into the distance, leaving only a settling cloud of dust like a soft golden blanket, Pecan cautiously poked his head out. The plains were quiet once more, peaceful and serene. He looked over at Thorn, who was perched on a nearby sun-warmed rock, the same sky overhead, the same grass below. Thorn looked down. His tummy fluttered once, then settled.

“Thorn,” Pecan said, his voice filled with deep and sincere admiration. “You did it. You were amazing. You saved us all.”

Thorn looked down at his wings, then up at the vast open sky that had seemed so daunting just moments before. The wind still blew, a gentle caress now. He had carried the warning, no matter the wind or the height. That felt even better than the loudest, happiest song he had ever sung. He smiled, a wide bright smile that reached all the way to his beady little eyes, and when he sang next it was from the rock, not from hiding in the grass.
